author: e. m. conner
title: Rounds discusses tribal radio funding with Interior Secretary at Senate subcommittee hearing
text:
U.S. Senator Mike Rounds discussed funding for tribal radio stations with Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum during a Senate Appropriations Committee’s Subcommittee on Interior, Environment and Related Agencies hearing on Apr. 22.
The discussion focused on the importance of continued support for tribally operated or affiliated radio stations in Indian country, which play a critical role in providing essential and emergency information to tribal communities.
“I was glad to see that the Bureau of Indian Affairs’ FY27 budget request does support funding for tribally operated or affiliated radio stations in Indian country,” Rounds said. “Can you share just how important it is for these tribal radio stations to continue to be funded?”
Burgum responded by highlighting the unique communication challenges faced by rural tribal areas. “I think as anybody who’s spent time in Indian country in states like ours in the West, Senator, know that landlines are not a thing in many parts of the rural residence,” Burgum said. “Cell service is often sketchy, even though some of the tribes do run their own cellular programs.” He added, “Radio is often sometimes the only way people can reach information, whether it’s winter storms or tornadoes, prairie fires… there’s real need for emergency information to be distributed to a population. I know that the tribal chairs and tribal councils all count on this for getting information out, not just about emergencies but about events going on in the community and about important things that tribal members need to know.”
Rounds has previously secured funding for these stations after it was proposed for elimination from a rescissions package last year. In addition to his work on appropriations related to Indian affairs, Rounds serves on several other Senate committees including Armed Services; Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs; Intelligence; and Appropriations according to his official website.
Rounds is a lifelong South Dakotan who grew up as the eldest of 11 children in Huron and has four children and eleven grandchildren according to his official website. He earned a bachelor’s degree in political science from South Dakota State University according to his official website and served two terms as governor before joining the U.S. Senate according to his official website.
During this hearing, Rounds also asked questions regarding construction of a new school on Cheyenne River reservation and about law enforcement funding.
